I more or less agree with this as well. I don't think that they are mutually exclusive definitions. I do take exception, however, to the assumption that fascism is related to socialism. Socialism is social ownership of the means of production. The core of socialism is not state ownership of the means of production. Marxist-Leninism made the argument that state ownership is social ownership, but that is heavily contested. Most socialists see democracy as a necessary precursor to social ownership. A good half of socialists believe that the existence of a state is antagonistic towards socialist organization. The vast majority of socialists today define socialism as "direct worker management of the means of production." IOW, socialism is the union owning and running the shop, instead of the union negotiating with the owners of the shop. As defined here, socialism is the complete opposite of fascism, as you defined it.

The second definition isn't really equating fascism to socialism, it's just pointing out how fascism has some similar economic goals to socialism (at least the Marxist-Leninist version) but accomplishes them differently.

For example, a socialist regime will expropriate and nationalize a factory, whereas a fascist regime will cartelize it, begin making all the substantive decisions about production, but leave the owner in place as a powerless figurehead. The result is the same (central planning enforced by a dictatorship), but the path taken to get there is different.

Or take unions, for example. Under socialism, a union directly controls the means of production. Under fascism, unions are turned into arms of the government and are included in the cartels. Again, same result (more union control over the economy) but different tactics.
